hints: Focus on what Fehling's solution actually tests for, aldehydes or ketones, and what colour change means a positive result.
Look carefully at the end of each carbonyl group in P, Q and R to spot whether it is -CHO or -COCH3.
Remember that a molecule counts as positive if it has at least one aldehyde group, even if it also contains a ketone group.
walkthrough:
**Identify the functional groups in P, Q and R**

Look at what is attached to each C=O carbon. If it is H on one side, it is an aldehyde. If it is C on both sides, it is a ketone.

P has $\text{CH}_3\text{C=O}$ on the left and $\text{HC=O}$ on the right, so it is a keto-aldehyde.

Q has $\text{HC=O}$ on both sides, so it is a dialdehyde.

R has $\text{CH}_3\text{C=O}$ on both sides, so it is a diketone.

**Recall how Fehling's solution works**

Fehling's contains blue $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ complex. On warming, aldehydes are easily oxidised and reduce $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to red-brown $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ precipitate.

$$\text{R-CHO} + 2\text{Cu}^{2+} + 5\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{R-COO}^- + \text{Cu}_2\text{O} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Ketones are not oxidised under these mild conditions, so they stay blue with no precipitate.

**Apply the test to P, Q and R**

P contains an aldehyde group, so positive. Q contains two aldehyde groups, so positive. R contains only ketone groups, so negative.

Therefore only P and Q form the red-brown precipitate.

options.A: Incorrect. R is pentane-2,4-dione with two ketone groups and no -CHO group. Ketones do not reduce Fehling's solution, so R stays blue.
options.B: Correct. P has one aldehyde plus one ketone, and Q has two aldehydes. Both can be oxidised and give red-brown Cu2O. R is a diketone only and gives a negative result.
options.C: Incorrect. It is true P is positive, but Q is also positive. Students who miss that Q is a dialdehyde with two -CHO groups may wrongly choose P only.
options.D: Incorrect. Q alone is positive, but P is also positive because one aldehyde group is enough. The extra ketone in P does not stop the aldehyde from reacting.
